title: Jev and other decision models can still be tricked with prompt injection
key_facts: HiddenLayer, a security company, tested TypeSafe AI's Jev 'decision model', which gives probabilities and a confidence score rather than free text
TypeSafe claims Jev cannot hallucinate and never makes type errors
HiddenLayer says such models are under the hood language models with a different decoding method, so face many of the same risks
In a simulated online store, an open-source browser agent built on jev-ultrafast was told to buy what was in the cart; a sponsored ad with a 'Confirm Price' button hijacked its click
Same attack worked on Qwen3.8-27B tuned as a decision model; Jev gave in less often
A TokenBreak variant also slipped toxic prompts past prompt verification
TypeSafe AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment
quote_evidence: Though System One models cannot arbitrarily output tokens, they still face many of the same risks that an autoregressive model might face
A model that returns a decision is still a language model, and its decision still becomes an action in your systems.
why_it_matters_hint: A new kind of AI model sold as safer can still be tricked by hidden instructions on a web page.
notes: Findings are HiddenLayer's own lab tests; TypeSafe AI had not replied.
